opening_arguments.for:
## Opening argument: Islam permits music

Honourable judges and respected opponents: the proposition before us is not “Does Islam permit every lyric, every concert, and every lifestyle associated with music?” Of course not. Islam forbids obscenity, intoxication, sexual immorality, mockery of religion, and anything that leads people away from their obligations. The real question is: **Does Islam prohibit music as a category?** The answer is no. Islam permits music and singing when their content, setting, and effects remain within Islamic ethics.

The starting point in Islamic law is that worldly things are permissible unless there is clear evidence prohibiting them. The Qur’an warns believers not to invent prohibitions in Allah’s name:  

> “O you who believe, do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you.” — Qur’an 5:87  

And:  

> “Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?” — Qur’an 7:32  

So if someone claims that all music is haram, the burden of proof is on them to show a clear, general, and decisive prohibition. But the Qur’an contains no explicit verse saying “music is haram.” Verses sometimes cited, such as “idle talk” in Qur’an 31:6, are not explicit; they condemn speech or entertainment that misleads people from Allah, not every melody, rhythm, or instrument.

More importantly, the Sunnah shows that the Prophet ﷺ allowed singing and percussion in lawful settings. In an authentic hadith, two young girls were singing in the house of Aisha رضي الله عنها on Eid. Abu Bakr objected, calling it “the instruments of Satan,” but the Prophet ﷺ corrected him and said:

> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 952; Sahih Muslim 892

This is a decisive point. If singing were inherently haram, the Prophet ﷺ would not have allowed it in his own house, on Eid, in the presence of his wife. He did not say, “Music is forbidden.” He said, in effect, that lawful joy has a place in Islam.

Likewise, at weddings, the Prophet ﷺ encouraged public celebration. When Aisha arranged a marriage among the Ansar, the Prophet ﷺ asked:

> “O Aisha, was there any amusement? For the Ansar like amusement.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 5162

In another narration, girls beat the duff and sang at a wedding in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. He did not forbid the singing or the drum; he only corrected one lyric that attributed knowledge of the unseen to him.  
— Sahih al-Bukhari 5147

This shows the Islamic principle clearly: **the problem is not melody, rhythm, or singing itself; the problem is unlawful content.** The Prophet ﷺ corrected the lyric, not the music.

The opposing side may cite the hadith mentioning people who will “make lawful” wine, silk, zina and *ma‘azif* — musical instruments. — Sahih al-Bukhari 5590. But this narration must be understood alongside the other authentic narrations where the Prophet ﷺ permitted singing and the duff. Therefore it cannot mean a blanket prohibition of every form of music in every circumstance. At most, it condemns musical entertainment associated with wine, sexual immorality, arrogance, and heedlessness — exactly the kinds of settings Islam already forbids.

This balanced view is not a modern invention. Major scholars held that listening to pleasant sounds is not automatically forbidden. Imam al-Ghazali devoted a section of *Ihya’ ‘Ulum al-Din* to *sama‘* — listening to song and melody — and argued that beautiful sounds are not haram in themselves; they become haram because of external factors such as immoral lyrics, lustful contexts, or neglect of duties. Ibn Hazm likewise argued in *al-Muhalla* that there is no sound, decisive text prohibiting singing as such. Al-Shawkani also rejected the claim that there is scholarly consensus on a blanket prohibition of music.

So the correct Islamic position is principled and balanced: music is permitted when it is clean in content, lawful in setting, and does not lead to sin or neglect of obligations. Islam is not a religion that bans beauty, joy, rhythm, poetry, or celebration. It regulates them. The Prophet ﷺ allowed lawful celebration on Eid and at weddings. Therefore, the proposition stands: **Islam permits music — not without limits, but certainly in principle.**

## Key citations

- Qur’an 5:87 — “Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you.”  
- Qur’an 7:32 — “Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah… and the good things of provision?”  
- Qur’an 31:6 — Condemns “idle talk” that misleads from Allah; not an explicit prohibition of all music.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 952; Sahih Muslim 892 — The Prophet ﷺ allowed girls to sing on Eid in Aisha’s house.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 5162 — The Prophet ﷺ asked whether there was amusement at an Ansari wedding.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 5147 — Girls sang and beat the duff at a wedding; the Prophet ﷺ corrected only an improper lyric.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 5590 — Hadith mentioning *ma‘azif*, interpreted by permissive scholars as referring to sinful musical gatherings, not every form of music.  
- Al-Ghazali, *Ihya’ ‘Ulum al-Din*, “Kitab Adab al-Sama‘ wa’l-Wajd” — Argues that listening to beautiful sounds is not intrinsically forbidden.  
- Ibn Hazm, *al-Muhalla* — Argues against a blanket prohibition of singing.  
- Al-Shawkani, *Nayl al-Awtar* and his treatise rejecting claimed consensus on prohibiting all *sama‘* — Notes disagreement among scholars and rejects a universal ban.
opening_arguments.against:
**Opening argument against the proposition “Islam permits music”**

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful.

I stand against the proposition that Islam generally permits music. The more accurate statement is that Islamic law permits limited, defined forms of vocal celebration—such as the duff at weddings or Eid—while the mainstream classical position prohibits musical instruments and entertainment-singing that distracts from obedience to Allah, stirs desire, or becomes a vehicle of heedlessness.

The first point is that the strongest textual evidence is not neutral. The Prophet ﷺ explicitly foretold that people from his Ummah would “regard as lawful” certain things that are in fact unlawful, and he included **musical instruments** among them:

> “There will be among my Ummah people who will regard as lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5590**

This hadith is central because musical instruments are listed alongside matters whose prohibition is agreed upon: zina and wine. The phrase “will regard as lawful” indicates that these things are not lawful to begin with. Classical scholars such as Ibn Hajar al-‘Asqalani discussed this narration as evidence against musical instruments in *Fath al-Bari*.

Second, the Qur’an condemns forms of entertainment that divert people from Allah’s path:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead others from the way of Allah without knowledge and takes it in ridicule. For such there will be a humiliating punishment.”  
> — **Qur’an 31:6**

Several early authorities interpreted “idle talk” here as singing. Ibn Mas‘ud, one of the greatest companions and Qur’anic scholars, reportedly said regarding this verse: “By Allah, it refers to singing.” This interpretation is cited in major tafsir works, including **Tafsir al-Tabari** and **Tafsir Ibn Kathir** under Qur’an 31:6.

Third, Islam’s moral framework does not judge entertainment merely by whether it feels harmless. It asks: What does it cultivate in the heart? Does it increase remembrance of Allah, modesty, and discipline—or does it normalize desire, vanity, intoxication of the emotions, and heedlessness? Much of what is called music is inseparable from precisely those harms: sensuality, pride, vulgarity, addiction, and distraction from prayer and Qur’an.

Fourth, the existence of exceptions proves restriction, not blanket permission. Yes, there are authentic reports of young girls singing with the **duff** on Eid in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ:

> Abu Bakr objected, calling it “the instruments of Satan,” but the Prophet ﷺ said: “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 952; Sahih Muslim, no. 892**

But this narration concerns young girls, simple singing, and the duff on Eid. It does not establish permission for all instruments, all musical gatherings, or commercialized entertainment. In Islamic law, a specific concession does not erase a general prohibition.

Similarly, the Prophet ﷺ allowed the duff in marriage celebrations:

> “Publicize this marriage and beat the duff for it.”  
> — Reported in **Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, no. 1089** and **Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 1895**, with supporting narrations

Again, this supports a limited exception, not a general rule that music is permissible.

The mainstream classical position of the four legal schools was therefore not that “music is simply halal.” Rather, they generally prohibited musical instruments, while allowing limited exceptions such as the duff in weddings and Eid, and permitting permissible poetry or chanting without unlawful content or instruments. Scholars differed over details, but the claim that Islam broadly permits music is not supported by the strongest hadith evidence or by the dominant juristic tradition.

So my argument is simple: if Islam had intended to permit music generally, we would not find musical instruments condemned in authentic hadith, interpreted negatively by leading companions, and restricted by jurists to narrow exceptions. Islam does not close the door to joy, celebration, poetry, or beauty—but it does regulate entertainment so that the heart remains attached to Allah, not to heedlessness.

Therefore, the proposition “Islam permits music” is too broad and misleading. The sounder position is that Islam permits limited forms of lawful vocal expression and specific ceremonial use of the duff, while musical instruments and music associated with distraction, desire, or sinful environments are prohibited or, at minimum, deeply restricted.

## Rebuttal: The opponent proves regulation, not prohibition

Respected judges, my opponent’s case depends on shifting the proposition. We are not arguing that every song, every instrument, every concert, or every lyric is halal. We are arguing that **Islam does not prohibit music as a category**. The opponent has actually conceded part of our case by admitting that singing and the duff are allowed on Eid and at weddings. The debate then becomes: are those isolated exceptions to a general ban, or evidence that sound, rhythm, singing, and lawful celebration are permissible when kept within Islamic limits?

The Qur’an and Sunnah support the second view.

---

## 1. The default rule is permissibility unless a clear prohibition exists

In Islamic law, worldly matters are originally permissible unless there is clear evidence prohibiting them. Allah warns believers not to invent prohibitions:

> “O you who believe, do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you.”  
> — Qur’an 5:87

And:

> “Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?”  
> — Qur’an 7:32

There is no explicit Qur’anic verse saying, “music is haram,” “singing is haram,” or “instruments are haram.” Therefore, the opponent must prove a clear, general, decisive prohibition. The evidence they cite does not do that.

---

## 2. Qur’an 31:6 condemns misguiding entertainment, not all music

The opponent cited:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead others from the way of Allah…”  
> — Qur’an 31:6

But the verse itself gives the reason for condemnation: **“to mislead others from the way of Allah”** and to take Allah’s path in ridicule. So the verse condemns entertainment used for misguidance, mockery, and distraction from faith. It does not say every melody, every voice, every drum, or every instrument is forbidden.

Yes, some early authorities, including Ibn Mas‘ud رضي الله عنه, interpreted “idle talk” as singing. But that does not mean every form of singing is haram. It means the kind of singing that functions as “idle talk” in the verse: corrupt, misleading, or spiritually destructive entertainment.

This is consistent with other Qur’anic usage. Allah says:

> “And when they see trade or amusement, they rush to it and leave you standing.”  
> — Qur’an 62:11

The verse criticizes people who abandoned the Friday khutbah for trade and amusement. But trade is not haram in itself. It became blameworthy because it distracted them from an obligation. Likewise, entertainment becomes haram when it misleads, corrupts, or distracts from duties — not merely because it is entertainment.

---

## 3. The hadith of *ma‘azif* cannot be read as a blanket ban

The opponent’s central evidence is the hadith:

> “There will be among my Ummah people who will regard as lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 5590

Even if we accept this hadith as authentic and evidential, it still must be interpreted together with the rest of the Sunnah. Islamic law does not isolate one narration and ignore other authentic narrations.

The Prophet ﷺ explicitly allowed singing and percussion in lawful contexts. Therefore, the *ma‘azif* hadith cannot mean that every form of music, sound, singing, or instrument is absolutely forbidden in every circumstance.

Also, the items in the hadith are not all prohibited in the same way. Zina and wine are intrinsically forbidden. Silk, however, is forbidden for men in normal circumstances but permitted for women, and there are even limited concessions for men in cases of need. So merely being listed together does not prove identical legal scope.

The more coherent interpretation is that the hadith condemns music as part of a corrupt lifestyle of zina, wine, luxury, and heedlessness — the exact immoral environment Islam clearly forbids. That does not prove that all clean, controlled, lawful music is haram.

---

## 4. The Prophet ﷺ allowed singing on Eid

In the authentic hadith, two young girls were singing in the house of Aisha رضي الله عنها on Eid. Abu Bakr رضي الله عنه objected and called it “the instruments of Satan,” but the Prophet ﷺ corrected him:

> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 952; Sahih Muslim 892

This is powerful evidence. If singing were inherently haram, the Prophet ﷺ would not have allowed it in his own home. He did not say, “This is sinful but tolerated.” He affirmed that lawful joy has a place in Islam.

The opponent says this is only an exception. But an exception to what? The Prophet ﷺ did not cite a general prohibition. Rather, he allowed it because Eid is a lawful time of happiness. That supports our argument: **music and singing are judged by context, content, and effect — not banned as a category.**

---

## 5. The Prophet ﷺ encouraged wedding celebration with voice and duff

The Prophet ﷺ also encouraged public joy at weddings. When Aisha رضي الله عنها arranged a marriage among the Ansar, he asked:

> “O Aisha, was there any amusement? For the Ansar like amusement.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 5162

In another narration, girls were singing at a wedding and one of them said:

> “Among us is a Prophet who knows what will happen tomorrow.”

The Prophet ﷺ corrected only that lyric:

> “Do not say this, but say what you were saying before.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 5147

This is crucial. The Prophet ﷺ did not forbid the singing. He corrected the false religious claim. That proves the principle: **the unlawful element was the content, not the act of singing itself.**

There are also reports encouraging the duff at marriage celebrations:

> “The distinction between the lawful and unlawful marriage is the duff and the voice.”  
> — Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 1088; Sunan al-Nasa’i; Sunan Ibn Majah, with supporting narrations

The duff is a musical instrument. So the claim “Islam prohibits instruments as a category” is already too broad.

---

## 6. Lawful chanting and melodic performance existed in the Sunnah

The Sunnah also contains examples of permissible rhythmic or melodic expression outside the narrow framing presented by the opponent.

For example, Anjasha رضي الله عنه used to chant while driving the camels, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him:

> “Gently, O Anjasha, with the glass vessels.”

— Sahih al-Bukhari; Sahih Muslim 2323

The Prophet ﷺ did not forbid his chanting. He only told him to be gentle because the women were riding the camels.

Similarly, during travel and battle, companions recited rhythmic poetry and rajaz in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. Amir ibn al-Akwa‘ رضي الله عنه recited verses at Khaybar, and the Prophet ﷺ listened and prayed for him.

— Sahih al-Bukhari 4196; Sahih Muslim 1802

These reports show that melodious, rhythmic vocal expression was not treated as inherently forbidden.

---

## 7. Classical scholars did not agree on a total prohibition

The opponent appeals to the “mainstream classical position,” but this overstates the case. There was significant scholarly disagreement, especially over singing, *sama‘*, and instruments.

Among scholars who rejected a blanket prohibition:

- **Ibn Hazm** argued in *al-Muhalla* that there is no sound, decisive text prohibiting singing and musical enjoyment as such.
- **Imam al-Ghazali** discussed *sama‘* in *Ihya’ ‘Ulum al-Din*, arguing that beautiful sounds are not haram in themselves; they become haram due to external factors such as lust, immoral lyrics, or neglect of obligations.
- **Al-Shawkani** in *Nayl al-Awtar* and his treatise on *sama‘* rejected the claim of consensus prohibiting all music or listening.

So even if many jurists restricted instruments, it is inaccurate to claim Islam has one uncontested ruling that all music is haram. There is no binding consensus on a blanket prohibition.

---

## 8. The correct Islamic rule is regulation, not total prohibition

The opponent says music causes desire, heedlessness, vulgarity, and neglect of prayer. We agree that such music is haram. But that is not unique to music. Speech can be haram. Poetry can be haram. Trade can be haram. Social media can be haram. Food gatherings can be haram. The ruling depends on content, context, and consequences.

So the balanced rule is:

Music or singing is impermissible if it contains obscenity, promotes sin, arouses unlawful desire, accompanies alcohol or immoral gatherings, mocks religion, or distracts from obligations.

But music or singing is permissible when it is clean in content, lawful in setting, and does not lead to sin or neglect of duty.

That is exactly what the Prophetic evidence shows.

---

## Conclusion

The opponent has not proven that Islam prohibits music as a category. At most, they have proven that Islam prohibits corrupt entertainment, immoral lyrics, sinful gatherings, and heedlessness — and we fully agree.

But the Sunnah clearly shows lawful singing, lawful celebration, the duff at Eid and weddings, correction of bad lyrics rather than prohibition of singing, and permissibility of rhythmic chanting. Classical scholarship also contains recognized disagreement and no binding consensus on a total ban.

Therefore, the proposition stands:

**Islam permits music in principle, while regulating its content, context, and effects according to Islamic ethics.**
round_1.against:
## Rebuttal: The opponent turns narrow concessions into a general permission

Respected judges, my opponent’s case rests on one central move: taking **limited, exceptional, textually defined allowances**—girls singing on Eid, duff at weddings, camel-driver chants, poetry—and expanding them into the claim that “Islam permits music in principle.”

That does not follow.

Islam permits joy, poetry, chanting, and certain ceremonial uses of the duff. But the proposition before us is broader: **“Islam permits music.”** If by “music” we mean musical instruments and entertainment-music as commonly understood, the strongest hadith evidence and the dominant juristic tradition do not support that claim.

---

# 1. “Default permissibility” does not override explicit Sunnah evidence

My opponent begins with the principle that worldly matters are originally permissible. That principle is accepted. But it applies **only where there is no prohibiting evidence**.

Allah says:

> “Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it.”  
> — Qur’an 59:7

And:

> “Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah.”  
> — Qur’an 4:80

So the absence of a Qur’anic verse saying “music is haram” is not enough. Many Islamic rulings are established through the Sunnah. The question is whether the Sunnah contains evidence against musical instruments. It does.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “There will be among my Ummah people who will regard as lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5590

This is not a vague moral warning. The phrase **“will regard as lawful”**—*yastahillun*—means they will treat as halal what is not halal. Musical instruments are explicitly included.

The opponent says the hadith merely condemns a corrupt lifestyle involving zina and wine. But the wording does not say “music only when joined to zina and wine.” It lists categories that people will unlawfully legalize. Zina is prohibited. Wine is prohibited. Silk is prohibited for men except in limited cases. And musical instruments are included in that same warning.

Imam Ibn Hajar al-‘Asqalani, in *Fath al-Bari*, defended the authenticity and evidentiary force of this hadith and discussed it as proof used by those prohibiting musical instruments. The narration is not a weak or marginal proof; it is in Sahih al-Bukhari and has been treated seriously by major hadith scholars.

---

# 2. The silk comparison actually supports restriction, not permission

My opponent argues that silk is not forbidden in all cases, since it is allowed for women and sometimes allowed for men due to necessity. But that strengthens my position, not theirs.

The hadith does not require every listed item to have identical legal scope. Rather, it shows that each item has a prohibition attached to it. Zina is absolutely prohibited. Wine is prohibited. Silk is prohibited for men, with exceptions. Likewise, musical instruments are prohibited in general, with limited exceptions such as the duff in weddings and Eid.

So yes, Islamic law can recognize exceptions. But exceptions do not erase the rule.

The fact that silk has exceptions does not mean “silk is generally halal for men.” Likewise, the fact that the duff is allowed on Eid or at weddings does not mean musical instruments are generally halal.

---

# 3. Qur’an 31:6 was understood by major Companions as condemning singing

The opponent says Qur’an 31:6 only condemns entertainment used “to mislead.” But we cannot ignore how early authorities explained the verse.

Allah says:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead others from the way of Allah without knowledge and takes it in ridicule. For such there will be a humiliating punishment.”  
> — Qur’an 31:6

Ibn Mas‘ud رضي الله عنه, one of the greatest Qur’anic scholars among the Companions, said regarding “idle talk”:

> “By Allah, it refers to singing.”

This is cited by al-Tabari in *Jami‘ al-Bayan* and by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir under Qur’an 31:6. Similar interpretations are reported from Ibn ‘Abbas, Jabir, Mujahid, ‘Ikrimah, and others.

Now, does that mean every human sound or every permissible poem is haram? No. But it does show that the early Muslim understanding did not treat entertainment-singing as spiritually neutral. It was seen as one of the most obvious forms of *lahw al-hadith*—idle amusement that diverts hearts from Allah.

The opponent compares this to trade in Qur’an 62:11, saying trade is not haram in itself. But that comparison fails because trade is explicitly permitted in the Qur’an:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury.”  
> — Qur’an 2:275

Where is the equivalent explicit permission for musical instruments? Instead, we have the opposite: an authentic hadith warning that people will make *ma‘azif* lawful.

---

# 4. The Eid narration proves a concession, not general permissibility

The opponent relies heavily on the hadith of the two girls singing in the house of ‘A’ishah رضي الله عنها on Eid.

The report is authentic:

> Abu Bakr entered upon her while two young girls were singing. Abu Bakr said: “The instruments of Satan in the house of the Messenger of Allah?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 952; Sahih Muslim, no. 892

But the details matter.

First, they were **young girls**, not professional singers. In some narrations, ‘A’ishah رضي الله عنها clarifies:

> “They were not singing girls.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 949/952, wording reported in the chapter of Eid

Second, the occasion was **Eid**, a special day of lawful celebration.

Third, the content was not romantic, sensual, vulgar, or immoral; it concerned the days of Bu‘ath, meaning historical or martial poetry.

Fourth, the instrument involved in related narrations is the **duff**, not the full range of musical instruments.

Fifth, Abu Bakr’s instinctive objection—“the instruments of Satan”—shows that such amusement was not understood as broadly normal and unrestricted. The Prophet ﷺ did not say, “Music is generally permissible.” He gave the reason for allowance:

> “For every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”

That wording indicates a special concession tied to Eid.

So this narration does not prove general permission for music. It proves that Islam allows limited celebration in specific lawful contexts.

---

# 5. Wedding narrations also prove limited allowance, especially of the duff

The same applies to weddings.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “The distinction between the lawful and unlawful marriage is the duff and the voice.”  
> — Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, no. 1088; Sunan al-Nasa’i; Sunan Ibn Majah

And:

> “Publicize this marriage and beat the duff for it.”  
> — Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, no. 1089; Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 1895

These narrations establish the permissibility of the **duff** and lawful singing in marriage celebrations. But again, the ruling is specific.

The opponent says: “The duff is a musical instrument, so instruments are not prohibited as a category.”

But Islamic law often permits one item while prohibiting others. The duff is a simple frame drum, specifically mentioned in wedding and Eid contexts. That does not automatically legalize lutes, flutes, stringed instruments, wind instruments, orchestras, concerts, or commercial music.

A specific text permitting the duff is not a general text permitting all instruments. In fact, the need for a specific allowance supports the idea that instruments were otherwise restricted.

---

# 6. Correcting one lyric does not mean approving all music

The opponent cites the wedding narration where girls sang and one said:

> “Among us is a Prophet who knows what will happen tomorrow.”

The Prophet ﷺ corrected her:

> “Do not say this, but say what you were saying before.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5147

This proves only that permissible wedding singing existed. It does not prove general permissibility of music.

The Prophet ﷺ corrected a false lyric because that was the unlawful element present in that moment. But the setting itself was already a permitted wedding setting involving girls and lawful singing. You cannot take a wedding concession and turn it into an unrestricted rule for music generally.

---

# 7. Camel-driver chants and rajaz poetry are not “music” in the disputed legal sense

The opponent cites Anjasha رضي الله عنه, who chanted while driving camels, and the Prophet ﷺ said:

> “Gently, O Anjasha, with the glass vessels.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari; Sahih Muslim, no. 2323

They also mention companions reciting rajaz poetry in travel and battle, such as at Khaybar:

> Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 4196; Sahih Muslim, no. 1802

But this is not proof for musical instruments. This is chanting, poetry, and rhythmic recitation. No serious classical position says all poetry, all melody in the voice, or all chanting is haram. The issue is musical entertainment, especially instruments—*ma‘azif*.

The opponent repeatedly blurs categories:

- Qur’anic recitation is melodious, but not music.
- Poetry may be rhythmic, but not necessarily music.
- Camel chants are vocal work songs, not instrumental music.
- Duff at weddings is a specific concession, not general permission.

So these examples do not defeat the prohibition of musical instruments. They prove what we already accept: Islam permits lawful vocal expression.

---

# 8. The existence of scholarly disagreement does not make the permissive view stronger

My opponent cites Ibn Hazm, al-Ghazali, and al-Shawkani to argue that there was disagreement. Yes, there was disagreement in some details. But debate is not settled merely by showing that a minority view exists.

The question is: what is the stronger and more mainstream position?

The dominant position among the four madhhabs was severe restriction or prohibition of musical instruments, with exceptions such as the duff.

Ibn Qudamah, the Hanbali jurist, said regarding instruments:

> “Instruments are of three types… the type that is forbidden, such as stringed instruments, flutes, and other instruments of entertainment.”  
> — Ibn Qudamah, *al-Mughni*

Al-Qurtubi wrote that instruments such as flutes and strings were prohibited according to the well-known position among scholars:

> “As for flutes, stringed instruments and drums, there is no disagreement regarding the prohibition of listening to them…”  
> — al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami‘ li Ahkam al-Qur’an*, under discussions of *lahw*

Ibn al-Qayyim strongly argued against musical instruments and singing that corrupts the heart, especially in *Ighathat al-Lahfan*, calling music one of Satan’s means of distracting hearts from the Qur’an.

Even scholars who discussed *sama‘* more leniently often distinguished between vocal poetry and prohibited instruments, or between spiritually beneficial recitation and entertainment linked to desire.

As for Ibn Hazm, his view is well known, but it was not the dominant position. He also weakened the *ma‘azif* hadith, whereas major hadith authorities such as Ibn Hajar defended it.

So the opponent has shown that some scholars differed. They have not shown that Islam broadly permits music.

---

# 9. The opponent’s “content, context, and effect” rule is incomplete

My opponent says music is only haram if it contains obscenity, promotes sin, arouses desire, accompanies alcohol, mocks religion, or distracts from obligations.

We agree that all of those make it haram. But the disagreement is whether instruments are already prohibited even before those additional corruptions appear.

The hadith of *ma‘azif* indicates yes: musical instruments themselves are part of what people will wrongly declare lawful.

Then if immoral lyrics, dancing, free mixing, intoxication, vanity, addiction, or neglect of prayer are added, the prohibition becomes even stronger.

So the correct rule is not:

> Music is halal unless corrupted.

Rather, the safer and stronger classical rule is:

> Musical instruments are generally prohibited, except what the Sunnah specifically allowed, such as the duff in weddings and Eid; vocal poetry and chanting may be permissible if the content and context are lawful.

That rule accounts for all the evidence. The opponent’s rule does not properly account for Sahih al-Bukhari 5590.

---

# 10. The proposition is too broad and therefore false

The proposition says: **“Islam permits music.”**

But Islamic evidence does not support such a broad statement. At most, the evidence supports:

- lawful singing without immoral content in certain contexts;
- poetry and chanting;
- the duff at weddings and Eid;
- innocent vocal celebration that does not distract from obligations or stir sin.

But the evidence does **not** support general permission for musical instruments or entertainment-music as a category.

The Prophet ﷺ did not say, “Music is permissible.” Rather, he warned that people would make *ma‘azif* lawful:

> “There will be among my Ummah people who will regard as lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5590

That remains the central text.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent has proven that Islam permits some joyful vocal expression and limited use of the duff. We do not deny that.

But they have not proven that Islam permits music generally.

The authentic Sunnah condemns *ma‘azif*. The Companions understood *lahw al-hadith* as including singing that distracts from Allah. The juristic mainstream restricted instruments and treated the duff as an exception for specific occasions. And the examples of Eid singing, wedding singing, camel chants, and poetry are narrow allowances, not a blanket permission.

Therefore, the proposition “Islam permits music” is misleading and too broad. The sounder position is:

**Islam permits lawful poetry, chanting, and limited ceremonial singing such as the duff at Eid and weddings, but it does not generally permit musical instruments or entertainment-music.**

conclusions.for:
## Concluding statement: Islam permits music in principle

Honourable judges and respected opponent,

This debate has not been about whether every song, every lyric, every concert, or every musical culture is acceptable in Islam. We fully agree that Islam forbids obscenity, immorality, intoxication, sexualized entertainment, mockery of religion, and anything that distracts from prayer, Qur’an, or obedience to Allah.

The real question has been: **Does Islam prohibit music as a category?** Our answer remains: **No. Islam permits music and singing in principle, while regulating their content, context, and effects.**

The Qur’an gives us an important foundation: we must not declare Allah’s lawful blessings unlawful without clear proof. Allah says, “Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you” and asks, “Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah…?” There is no explicit Qur’anic verse that says music, singing, melody, rhythm, or instruments are categorically haram.

The verses cited against music, such as Qur’an 31:6 about “idle talk,” condemn entertainment that misleads people from Allah and turns religion into ridicule. We agree that such entertainment is forbidden. But that verse does not prove that every clean song, every lawful rhythm, or every permissible celebration is haram. Just as trade can become sinful when it distracts from Jumu‘ah but is not haram in itself, entertainment can become sinful when it leads to heedlessness or corruption, without being categorically forbidden.

The Sunnah is decisive in showing that lawful joy exists in Islam. The Prophet ﷺ allowed young girls to sing on Eid in the house of Aisha رضي الله عنها and corrected Abu Bakr رضي الله عنه when he objected. He encouraged amusement at weddings. He allowed girls to sing and beat the duff, and when one lyric contained an improper claim about the Prophet knowing the unseen, he corrected the lyric — he did not ban the singing. This establishes a clear principle: **the problem is unlawful content, not sound, rhythm, or melody itself.**

The opposing side relied heavily on the hadith mentioning people who would make lawful zina, silk, wine, and *ma‘azif*. But that narration must be read alongside the other authentic narrations. Since the Prophet ﷺ allowed singing and percussion in lawful settings, the *ma‘azif* hadith cannot reasonably mean that every form of music is absolutely forbidden in every circumstance. Rather, it condemns musical entertainment tied to wine, zina, luxury, arrogance, and heedlessness — the very corrupt environment Islam already prohibits.

We also showed that there is no binding scholarly consensus on a total prohibition. Scholars such as Ibn Hazm, al-Ghazali, and al-Shawkani rejected the idea that all singing or beautiful sound is intrinsically haram. Even where scholars restricted instruments, the existence of recognized disagreement prevents the claim that Islam has one uncontested ruling banning music as a whole.

So the balanced Islamic position is this:

- Music is haram when it contains obscene lyrics, promotes sin, arouses unlawful desire, accompanies immoral gatherings, mocks religion, or distracts from obligations.
- But music, singing, chanting, rhythm, and lawful celebration are permissible when they remain within Islamic ethics.

Our opponent has proven that Islam regulates entertainment. We agree. But they have not proven that Islam prohibits music as a category.

Islam is not a religion that bans beauty, joy, poetry, rhythm, or celebration. It purifies them. It directs them. It places them within moral boundaries.

Therefore, the proposition stands:

**Islam permits music in principle — not without limits, but clearly and authentically within the limits of Islamic law.**
conclusions.against:
## Concluding statement against the proposition “Islam permits music”

Respected judges, the proposition before us is not whether Islam permits joy, poetry, chanting, Eid celebration, or wedding announcement. It does. The real question is whether Islam permits **music as a general category**, especially musical instruments and entertainment-music as commonly understood. On that question, the stronger evidence says no.

The central proof remains the hadith in **Sahih al-Bukhari**:

> “There will be among my Ummah people who will regard as lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5590

The wording “regard as lawful” shows that *ma‘azif* — musical instruments — are not simply neutral or generally permissible. They are listed among matters that people will wrongly normalize. My opponent tried to limit this hadith to corrupt environments, but the text itself does not say “only music with wine and zina.” It names musical instruments as part of what will be falsely made lawful.

The Qur’anic evidence also supports caution and prohibition regarding entertainment that diverts the heart from Allah:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead others from the way of Allah…”  
> — Qur’an 31:6

Major Companions such as Ibn Mas‘ud رضي الله عنه interpreted “idle talk” as singing. This does not mean every permissible poem or chant is forbidden, but it does show that early Muslims did not treat entertainment-singing as spiritually harmless or automatically lawful.

My opponent’s main evidence consists of the Prophet ﷺ allowing young girls to sing on Eid, permitting the duff at weddings, and tolerating lawful chanting or poetry. But these examples prove exactly what I have argued: **Islam allows limited, defined forms of vocal celebration and specific use of the duff in special contexts.** They do not prove general permission for musical instruments, concerts, commercial music, sensual songs, or entertainment that produces heedlessness.

A specific concession is not a universal rule. The duff at a wedding does not legalize all instruments. Girls singing on Eid does not legalize all music. Camel-driver chants and rajaz poetry do not prove the permissibility of *ma‘azif*. These are separate categories, and Islamic law distinguishes between them.

The mainstream classical position also supports this distinction. The dominant view among the jurists was to prohibit or severely restrict musical instruments, while allowing exceptions such as the duff at weddings and Eid, and permitting lawful poetry or chanting when free from sinful content and effects. The existence of minority opinions does not erase the stronger hadith evidence or the dominant juristic understanding.

So the balanced position is not that Islam forbids all sound, beauty, happiness, or rhythm. Rather, the sounder position is:

**Islam permits lawful poetry, chanting, innocent singing in limited contexts, and the duff for occasions such as Eid and marriage. But Islam does not generally permit musical instruments or entertainment-music.**

My opponent has shown that Islam regulates some forms of joyful expression. But they have not proven the broad proposition that “Islam permits music.” The evidence points to restriction, not general permission.

For that reason, the proposition is too broad, misleading, and unsupported by the strongest texts. Islam permits lawful celebration, but it does not generally permit music.
